notice: Static recorded assessment output. Not a live scan. Values are taken from a genuine sandbox run on 28 October 2026 for example.com; profiles for the other four approved domains are reference profiles shipped with runtime v5.2.0.

controls.name: Address resolution and record presence
controls.evaluates: Whether the apex name publishes resolvable A and AAAA records, whether the answers are consistent across resolvers, and whether the name is reachable at all.
controls.why: Everything else in an external assessment depends on this. A name that does not resolve is either a misconfiguration or an outage - both are visible to customers before they are visible internally.

controls.name: DNSSEC chain validation
controls.evaluates: Whether the zone is signed, whether a DS record exists at the parent, and whether the chain validates when queried through a validating resolver.
controls.why: Without DNSSEC, a forged DNS answer is indistinguishable from a real one for most clients. It does not encrypt traffic; it makes tampering detectable.
controls.example: Zone signed with validated RRSIG and parent DS delegation.

controls.name: CAA authorisation
controls.evaluates: Whether the domain publishes CAA records, which certificate authorities they name, and whether the policy includes a reporting address.
controls.why: CAA restricts which CAs may issue for your name. It reduces - but does not eliminate - the chance of an unauthorised certificate being issued by a compliant CA.
controls.example: example.org. 300 IN CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"

controls.name: Zone transfer exposure
controls.evaluates: Whether each authoritative nameserver answers an AXFR or IXFR request from an unauthorised client.
controls.why: A zone that transfers to anyone publishes the complete map of internal hostnames and services. Modern DNS servers refuse this by default; older or misconfigured ones do not.
controls.example: AXFR example.org @ns1.example.org -> REFUSED (expected); IXFR -> NOTIMP

controls.name: Name record hygiene
controls.evaluates: Dangling CNAMEs, records pointing at decommissioned hosting, orphaned service records and unexpected wildcard answers.
controls.why: A record that points at a name nobody controls any more is the classic subdomain-takeover path. It is quiet, cheap to fix and easy to miss from inside.
controls.example: www.example.org. CNAME shop.example-host.io. -> NXDOMAIN (hosting account closed)

controls.name: SPF policy strength
controls.evaluates: Whether an SPF record exists at the apex, which mechanisms it authorises, and whether the policy ends in a hard fail (-all), a soft fail (~all), or no enforcement at all.
controls.why: SPF tells receiving servers which hosts may send your mail. A soft policy tells them to be suspicious; a hard fail tells them to reject.
controls.example: v=spf1 -all (strict no-mail policy for reserved domain).

controls.name: SPF record validity
controls.evaluates: Multiple SPF records, recursive lookup count against the RFC 7208 limit of 10 DNS-querying mechanisms, void lookups, and syntax errors that cause permerror.
controls.why: An SPF record that errors out is worse than a simple strict one: receivers fall back to a permerror result and policy enforcement becomes unpredictable.
controls.example: 2 TXT records matched v=spf1 -> permerror per RFC 7208 section 4.5

controls.name: DMARC enforcement
controls.evaluates: The published _dmarc policy (none, quarantine or reject), the subdomain policy, alignment modes (adkim/aspf), and the reporting addresses.
controls.why: DMARC is the policy layer: it tells receivers what to do when SPF or DKIM fails. p=none asks for reports; p=reject actually stops spoofed mail.
controls.example: v=DMARC1; p=reject; sp=reject; adkim=s; aspf=s

controls.name: DKIM presence and key strength
controls.evaluates: Whether discoverable selectors publish keys, the key type and length, and whether weak or revoked keys are still in use.
controls.why: DKIM signs the message itself, so a forged message cannot carry a valid signature. Short or misconfigured keys weaken that guarantee.
controls.example: selector1._domainkey -> v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=... (2048-bit, rsa-sha256)

controls.name: MX and null-MX posture
controls.evaluates: Whether MX records exist, where they point, whether a null MX (RFC 7505) is published for domains that do not accept mail, and whether the routing is internally consistent.
controls.why: A domain that does not send mail should say so. A missing or contradictory MX is an invitation for forged mail to be delivered to a fallback host.
controls.example: MX 0 . published indicating domain does not accept e-mail.

controls.name: TLS protocol versions
controls.evaluates: Which protocol versions the endpoint negotiates, and whether deprecated versions (TLS 1.0/1.1, SSLv3) are still accepted.
controls.why: Old protocol versions carry known weaknesses and are deprecated by every major standards body. A modern baseline is TLS 1.2 with TLS 1.3 preferred.
controls.example: TLS 1.3 negotiated; TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 refused by the endpoint.

controls.name: Certificate validity and hostname coverage
controls.evaluates: Trust chain, expiry, hostname or SAN coverage, and whether the presented certificate is the one a browser will accept without a warning.
controls.why: An expired or mismatched certificate trains users to click through warnings - which is exactly the habit phishing relies on.
controls.example: Valid X.509 certificate covering example.com over TLS 1.3.

controls.name: Cipher suites and forward secrecy
controls.evaluates: Whether modern AEAD suites are offered, whether ephemeral key exchange (ECDHE) is available, and whether legacy CBC or export-grade suites remain enabled.
controls.why: Forward secrecy means a stolen private key cannot decrypt traffic recorded earlier. Legacy suites are the first thing removed in a hardening pass.
controls.example: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 preferred; ECDHE available; no CBC or RC4 suites offered.

controls.name: HTTPS redirect and downgrade path
controls.evaluates: Whether plain HTTP on port 80 redirects to HTTPS, whether the redirect is permanent, and whether any resource is still served unencrypted.
controls.why: A site that answers HTTP without redirecting gives an attacker on the path a free opportunity to intercept or rewrite the first request.
controls.example: http://example.org -> 301 https://example.org/ (single hop, no body served).

controls.name: Strict-Transport-Security
controls.evaluates: Whether HSTS is sent over HTTPS, the max-age it declares, whether it covers subdomains, and whether it is submitted for preloading.
controls.why: HSTS tells the browser to refuse plain HTTP for this host in future. It is the only control that protects the very first request of a later visit.
controls.example: Strict-Transport-Security header not enforced on reference landing page.

controls.name: Content-Security-Policy
controls.evaluates: Whether a CSP is present, whether it restricts script sources, and whether it uses unsafe-inline, unsafe-eval or a wildcard that would defeat the purpose.
controls.why: CSP is the main browser-side mitigation against cross-site scripting. It does not fix an injection bug, but it limits what the injected script can do.
controls.example: Content-Security-Policy header absent on static reference response.

controls.name: Clickjacking and MIME-sniffing protection
controls.evaluates: X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors, and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.
controls.why: Framing protection stops a page being embedded invisibly behind a click target. nosniff stops a browser guessing a content type and executing something it should not.
controls.example: X-Frame-Options: DENY; X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

controls.name: Referrer, permissions and version disclosure
controls.evaluates: Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, and whether Server or X-Powered-By headers advertise exact software versions.
controls.why: Version banners save an attacker reconnaissance. Referrer and permissions policies limit what a page leaks or is allowed to use on the visitor's device.
controls.example: Server: nginx/1.18.0 and X-Powered-By: PHP/7.4.3 disclosed in response headers.

controls.name: High-risk port reachability
controls.evaluates: Whether a defined set of high-risk services (FTP 21, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, direct database ports 3306/5432/6379/27017) accepts a TCP connection from the public internet.
controls.why: These services were never designed to face the internet. Reachability alone is a finding; the assessment never attempts authentication.
controls.example: TCP 3306 connection accepted from assessment vantage point (MySQL banner suppressed).

controls.name: SMB negotiate exposure (445)
controls.evaluates: Whether port 445 completes a single unauthenticated SMB2 negotiate, and which dialect and signing requirements are advertised in the response.
controls.why: SMB exposed to the internet is the ingress path behind several ransomware campaigns. The check reads the negotiate response only: no session, no shares, no credentials.
controls.example: SMB2 negotiate answered on 445; dialect 3.1.1; signing required -> service exposed.

controls.name: Remote Desktop reachability (3389)
controls.evaluates: Whether TCP 3389 accepts a connection and completes a protocol handshake, and whether the negotiated security layer is current.
controls.why: Internet-facing RDP is routinely brute-forced. Even with strong passwords, exposure widens the attack surface to anyone with a scanner.
controls.example: RDP negotiation answered on 3389 (NLA required) from the public internet.

controls.name: Database and admin interface exposure
controls.evaluates: Whether common management interfaces (phpMyAdmin, admin panels, Elasticsearch, Docker API) answer on standard ports without a network-level restriction.
controls.why: An admin panel reachable from the internet is one credential away from full control. Network restriction is usually the cheapest available fix.
controls.example: HTTP 200 with admin login form at :9200/_plugin/... on a public address.
